Server: the QUIC endpoint's anonymous HTTP/3 front runs Kestrel's race itself instead of drawing its answer from odds measured on one host. As soon as a request's HEADERS complete, the application's answer is queued on the thread pool, as Kestrel's Http3Stream does, while the parser keeps reading the body, frames and trailers, so a later frame error can still win while the 401 or 431 is being sent; the calibrated trailer schedule and its sampler are gone, and with them the extra hop before a 431 and the queued protocol abort. The response dispatch keeps the application's completion, the native write (bytes with FIN) and an abort apart, and joins them before the stream is released; a protocol error goes on the wire before native I/O is canceled. A completed response marks the reader stopped, then aborts the read side with H3_NO_ERROR, and only then cancels the read: a canceled read would make .NET send its default error code, and a parser the abort wakes inline would take it for a failure and cut the 401. A request's reader now grows from 4 KB to 16 KB only after it has consumed a full read; the control and QPACK readers stay at 4 KB. Tests gate the bytes or the response at the parser's and the application's boundaries instead of pinning a schedule, and the parity bursts sample independent connection pairs, 20 streams each. The parity suite has not been run on this code yet, and DATA-after-trailers stays an open difference, ours answering 401 more often (protocol-15.md, ip-blocking-release.md). Tested: VpnHood.Test's HTTP/3, request-proof and QUIC stream tests, also on this commit alone (written by Astra and Sol, reviewed by Claude in two rounds; IP-blocking plan item 5.6.6.3)
